items.stem: A historian finds this memo while researching why firms moved production abroad: 'Our Ohio plant pays $18/hour fully loaded. The Monterrey proposal pays $2.50/hour with comparable quality. Even after freight, we save 30%. The board expects a recommendation by Friday.' — internal company memo, 1995 (original composition for this item). What should the historian recognize about using this memo as evidence?

stimulus.text: Our Ohio plant pays $18/hour fully loaded. The Monterrey proposal pays $2.50/hour with comparable quality. Even after freight, we save 30%. The board expects a recommendation by Friday. — Internal company memo, 1995 (original composition for this item.)

options: (A) The memo is useless as evidence because it is a business document rather than a government record.
(B) The memo reveals nothing about why companies made offshoring decisions.
(C) The memo illustrates the cost logic behind one firm's decision, but a single company cannot by itself prove how widespread offshoring was.
(D) Business memos from this era are all forgeries and must be discarded.
items.explanation: The memo is valuable evidence of motive — it shows the wage arithmetic that made Mexico attractive after NAFTA lowered trade barriers. But one firm's decision does not establish a national trend; the historian would need many such sources, plus employment and trade data, to show the pattern was general.

option_explanations.A: Incorrect. Business records are legitimate primary sources for business history; the source's origin does not disqualify it.
option_explanations.B: Incorrect. The memo is explicit about motive: a 30 percent saving after freight costs drove the recommendation.
option_explanations.C: Correct. It states the proper scope of inference: vivid evidence of the mechanism in one case, which must be corroborated before generalizing.
option_explanations.D: Incorrect. There is no basis for dismissing all business memos as forgeries; sources are evaluated individually, not rejected by category.

items.stem: Which combination of developments best explains the long economic expansion of the 1990s, which the review calls 'the longest expansion on record to that point'?
options: (A) A return to the gold standard and the abolition of the income tax.
(B) Massive cuts to military spending that eliminated the entire federal budget.
(C) A ban on imported goods that forced all production back to American factories.
(D) Rising productivity from computers and the internet, expanding global trade, and budget agreements that moved the federal budget toward surplus.
items.explanation: The 1990s boom rested on several supports at once: information technology lifted productivity, NAFTA and the WTO opened markets, and the budget deals of 1990 and 1993 — tax increases plus spending restraint — combined with strong growth to produce surpluses. No single cause explains a decade-long expansion.

option_explanations.A: Incorrect. The United States did not return to the gold standard, and the income tax was not abolished; neither happened in the 1990s.
option_explanations.B: Incorrect. Defense spending fell after the Cold War but remained very large, and the budget was not eliminated — it moved into surplus through higher revenues and restraint.
option_explanations.C: Incorrect. The 1990s moved toward more open trade, not less; imports grew substantially during the expansion.
option_explanations.D: Correct. It names the three real pillars — the tech-driven productivity surge, trade expansion, and fiscal consolidation — that historians cite for the decade's growth.

items.stem: The review lists 'deregulation' among the causes of the 2008 financial crisis, and its key terms note that deregulation 'accelerated under Reagan across airlines, banking, energy, and communications.' Which line of causation connects Reagan-era banking deregulation to the 2008 crisis?
options: (A) Looser rules on banking let financial firms take bigger risks with borrowed money and mortgage-backed securities, amplifying the damage when the housing bubble burst.
(B) President Reagan personally approved every subprime mortgage issued in the 2000s.
(C) All deregulation was reversed in 1989, so it could not have had any later effects.
(D) The 2008 crisis was caused solely by the 1981 PATCO strike.
items.explanation: Deregulation removed many of the Depression-era limits on what banks and financial firms could do with depositors' money and borrowed funds. By the 2000s, lightly regulated firms had built enormous leveraged bets on housing; when home prices fell, the losses cascaded through the financial system far more violently than under the old rules.

option_explanations.A: Correct. It traces the mechanism: fewer restraints on risk-taking meant the housing downturn became a system-wide financial crisis rather than a contained housing slump.
option_explanations.B: Incorrect. Reagan left office in 1989, nearly two decades before the crisis; no president approves individual mortgages.
option_explanations.C: Incorrect. Much Reagan-era deregulation remained in place and was extended in later decades; it was not reversed in 1989.
option_explanations.D: Incorrect. The PATCO strike concerned air-traffic controllers in 1981 and had no causal connection to mortgage finance in 2008.

items.stem: As the WTO trading system expanded in the 1990s and 2000s, American consumers saw the prices of clothing, electronics, and household goods fall. This price drop is best explained by which of the following?
options: (A) The federal government set legal maximum prices on all imported goods.
(B) Competition from lower-cost producers abroad forced prices down across these product categories.
(C) American shoppers organized a nationwide boycott that forced every retailer to cut prices.
(D) Inflation ended permanently in the United States in 1995.
items.explanation: Open trade let retailers source from the cheapest producers worldwide. Foreign factories with far lower labor costs could sell clothing and electronics more cheaply than domestic makers, and competition among importers passed those savings to shoppers — the consumer side of globalization's bargain.

option_explanations.A: Incorrect. The United States did not impose price controls on imports; prices fell through market competition, not government decree.
option_explanations.B: Correct. Lower production costs abroad, transmitted through competitive retail markets, are the standard explanation for the era's falling goods prices.
option_explanations.C: Incorrect. No such nationwide boycott occurred; shoppers bought more imported goods, not fewer, as prices fell.
option_explanations.D: Incorrect. Inflation continued at low but positive rates; it did not end, permanently or otherwise.

items.stem: The chart shows union membership falling from 20.1 percent of U.S. workers in 1980 to 13.5 percent in 2000 — a decline of roughly one-third. As organized labor shrank, which political effect followed?

chart_spec.title: Union Membership as Share of U.S. Workers, 1980–2020
chart_spec.source_note: Approximate figures; union decline as a political-economic force, following the PATCO turning point in u9.md §Key terms.

options: (A) Unions grew steadily stronger as a share of all campaign spending.
(B) Union leaders took over the leadership of both major political parties.
(C) Organized labor's political muscle — votes mobilized, money raised, and workplaces organized — shrank, reducing workers' leverage in policymaking.
(D) The decline of unions had no political consequences of any kind.
items.explanation: Unions had been the Democratic Party's ground troops: registering voters, staffing phone banks, and funding campaigns. As membership fell by a third, that machinery withered, leaving working-class economic interests with less organized representation in Washington regardless of which party held power.

option_explanations.A: Incorrect. Union political spending and membership moved in the same downward direction; a shrinking movement did not command a growing share of campaign money.
option_explanations.B: Incorrect. Union leaders did not take over either party; if anything, both parties paid less attention to labor as its numbers fell.
option_explanations.C: Correct. It follows directly: fewer members means fewer dues, fewer volunteers, and fewer organized workplaces — the raw materials of political influence.
option_explanations.D: Incorrect. A one-third decline in one of the country's largest organized interest groups necessarily altered the political balance.

items.fact_source: u9.md §Key terms — PATCO strike (1981), 'a landmark defeat for organized labor'; §The story — breaking the strike 'to signal that organized labor's power was over'

items.stem: Which of the following jobs belongs to the service sector rather than the manufacturing sector?
options: (A) Assembling automobiles on a production line.
(B) Smelting steel in a mill.
(C) Operating a power loom in a textile factory.
(D) Providing home health care to elderly patients.
items.explanation: Service work provides a service rather than producing a tangible good. Home health care — like retail, food service, finance, and education — is performed for a customer directly, while the other three options all make physical products in factories.

option_explanations.A: Incorrect. Auto assembly produces a tangible good — cars — which is the definition of manufacturing work.
option_explanations.B: Incorrect. Smelting produces steel, a physical commodity, placing it squarely in manufacturing.
option_explanations.C: Incorrect. Operating a loom produces cloth, a manufactured good, not a service.
option_explanations.D: Correct. Home health aides deliver care, a service consumed at the moment it is provided, making it typical of the service economy that grew as manufacturing employment shrank.

items.fact_source: u9.md §The story — globalization-era restructuring of American employment

items.stem: The chart shows U.S. manufacturing employment at selected years. A historian studying factory towns would expect plant closings — and their local fallout of lost tax revenue, strained schools, and population loss — to have clustered most heavily in which period?

chart_spec.title: U.S. Manufacturing Employment, 1979–2000
chart_spec.source_note: Approximate figures consistent with the manufacturing job losses of the globalization era described in u9.md §The story and §What the exam tests here.

options: (A) 1979–1983, when employment fell by 2.7 million, the steepest drop shown on the chart.
(B) 1983–1989, when manufacturing employment was rising.
(C) 1993–2000, when employment held roughly steady.
(D) No period on the chart stands out from the others.
items.explanation: The 1979–83 fall of 2.7 million jobs is the sharpest decline plotted, reflecting the brutal combination of the early-1980s recessions and the first great wave of plant closings. Towns whose mills and factories shut in those years lost their tax base at once, setting off the downward spiral of shrinking services and out-migration.

option_explanations.A: Correct. Subtracting 16.7 from 19.4 gives the 2.7 million drop — larger than any other interval on the chart — so this is when the most plants were closing.
option_explanations.B: Incorrect. Employment rose from 16.7 to 17.9 million in these years, indicating net hiring rather than a wave of closings.
option_explanations.C: Incorrect. Employment was roughly flat from 1993 to 2000 (16.7 to 17.3 million), not collapsing.
option_explanations.D: Incorrect. The 1979–83 drop is visibly steeper than the other intervals, so one period clearly stands out.

items.fact_source: u9.md §The story — Reagan-era restructuring; §What the exam tests here — globalization's winners and losers

items.stem: The review says Reagan broke the 1981 PATCO strike 'to signal that organized labor's power was over.' A critic argues the strike's defeat was merely symbolic. Which evidence best supports the review's view that the defeat was substantive rather than merely symbolic?
options: (A) The strike's defeat had no effect on any employer's behavior in the following decade.

(B) The government kept air traffic running with replacement workers, demonstrating that even a strike by highly skilled workers could be broken — a lesson private employers then applied in their own labor disputes.
(C) Union membership rose sharply in the years immediately after 1981.
(D) The fired controllers were all rehired with back pay within a month.
items.explanation: PATCO mattered because it was a demonstration. Air-traffic controllers were skilled, hard-to-replace federal workers; when the government defeated them anyway, private employers took the lesson that aggressive anti-strike tactics — including hiring permanent replacements — would be tolerated, and strike activity fell sharply through the 1980s.

option_explanations.A: Incorrect. Employers visibly hardened their stance after 1981, demanding concessions and replacing strikers more aggressively than before.
option_explanations.B: Correct. It identifies the mechanism by which a single federal action changed private-sector behavior: a successful example that others copied.
option_explanations.C: Incorrect. Union membership fell, not rose, after 1981, which is consistent with the strike's defeat weakening labor.
option_explanations.D: Incorrect. The controllers were not rehired; they were fired and banned from federal service, which was precisely what made the example so stark.

items.stem: The chart shows the foreign-born share of the U.S. population from 1970 to 2020. Which statement best describes the trend?

chart_spec.title: Foreign-Born Share of U.S. Population, 1970–2020
chart_spec.source_note: Approximate census-based figures; the demographic change 'especially around immigration' described in u9.md §The story.

options: (A) The foreign-born share fell steadily after 1970.
(B) The foreign-born share stayed flat at about 5 percent across the whole period.
(C) Immigration had no measurable effect on the composition of the U.S. population.
(D) The foreign-born share nearly tripled between 1970 and 2020, rising from 4.7 to 13.7 percent.
items.explanation: The line rises in every decade shown, from 4.7 percent in 1970 to 13.7 percent in 2020 — roughly a threefold increase. This is the demographic transformation the review describes: immigration reshaping the nation's makeup and, with it, its politics.

option_explanations.A: Incorrect. The line rises continuously; no decade on the chart shows a decline.
option_explanations.B: Incorrect. The share was near 5 percent only in 1970; by 2020 it had climbed to 13.7 percent.
option_explanations.C: Incorrect. A near-tripling of the foreign-born share is a large compositional change by any measure.
option_explanations.D: Correct. It reports the chart's start and end values accurately (4.7 to 13.7 percent is just under triple) and describes the unbroken upward trend.

items.fact_source: u9.md §The story — 'demographic change — the coming "majority-minority" nation — reshaped politics, especially around immigration'

items.stem: The Immigration and Nationality Act of 1965 (the Hart-Celler Act) ended the national-origins quota system of the 1920s. The chart shows legal U.S. immigration by decade, 1960s–2000s. Which statement best connects the chart to the law's 'long tail'?

chart_spec.title: Legal U.S. Immigration by Decade, 1960s–2000s
chart_spec.source_note: Approximate figures; the post-1965 growth in immigration underlying the demographic change described in u9.md §The story ('especially around immigration').

options: (A) Each decade after the 1960s brought more legal immigrants than the one before, with the 1990s and 2000s far above pre-1965 levels — the long tail of the post-1965 system.
(B) Legal immigration effectively ended in the 1970s and never recovered.
(C) The 1960s saw the highest immigration of any decade shown on the chart.
(D) The chart shows that the 1965 law had no connection to later immigration levels.
items.explanation: The bars climb every decade: 3.3, 4.5, 6.0, 9.8, then 10.4 million. The 1965 law's family-reunification rules created a self-reinforcing system — each admitted immigrant could sponsor relatives — so the law's effects compounded for decades, producing the demographic reshaping the review describes.

option_explanations.A: Correct. It reads the chart's steady climb accurately and connects it to the mechanism — chain migration under family preferences — that made the 1965 act's consequences grow over time.
option_explanations.B: Incorrect. The chart shows the opposite: the 1970s brought 4.5 million, more than the 1960s' 3.3 million.
option_explanations.C: Incorrect. The 1960s bar (3.3 million) is the shortest on the chart, not the tallest.
option_explanations.D: Incorrect. The sustained growth beginning right after 1965 is precisely the law's long tail, not evidence of its irrelevance.
